## Introduction

So far we have introduced two of the "Three Cs" of general topology: continuity and connectedness.

In this chapter, we present the third: compact-ness.

This concept is not as intuitive as continuity or connectedness. In fact, a formal definition for compactness in a general topological space took some time for topologists to establish.

Compactness is the most important topological property. It plays a key role in many branches of mathematics.

It would be fair to say that "until you understand compactness you do not understand topology!"

So what is compactness? It could be described as the topologists generalization of finiteness.

## Compactness - Definition

::: block
### Definition 8.1

Let $A$ be a subset of a topological space $(X, \tau)$. Then $A$ is said to be compact if for every set $I$ and every family of open sets, $O_i$, $i \in I$, such that $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I}\,O_i$, there exists a finite subfamily $O_{i_1},O_{i_2},\dots,O_{i_n}$ such that $A\subseteq O_{i_1}\cup O_{i_2}\cup \dots \cup O_{i_n}$.
:::

In other words, imagine we have an infinite collection of open sets, and if we combine all of them, their union form a superset that contains $A$.

If $A$ is compact, we don't need that entire infinite collection. We can just pick out a finite number of those open sets, and their union will still be a superset of $A$.

And for $A$ to be officially compact, this rule must hold true for any infinite family of open sets that contains $A$.

## Compactness - Example

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
If $(X,\tau)=\mathbb{R}$ and $A=(0,\infty)$, then $A$ is **not** compact.
:::

\vspace{3mm}

**Proof.** For each positive integer $i$, let $O_i$ be the open interval $(0,i)$. Then, clearly, $A \subseteq \bigcup^\infty_{i=1} O_i$. But there do **not** exist $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n$ such that $A\subseteq (0,i_1)\cup(0,i_2)\cup\dots\cup(0,i_n)$. Therefore $A$ is not compact.

\vspace{4mm}

In other words, no matter how large we choose $n$, we cannot extract a finite subfamily whose union is a superset of $A$. This means $A\not\subseteq (0,i_1)\cup(0,i_2)\cup\dots\cup(0,i_n)$

For this specific family of open sets, the only way to form a superset of $A$ is by using the infinite union itself, $A \subseteq \bigcup^\infty_{i=1} O_i$.

## Compactness - Example

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Let $(X, \tau)$ be any topological space and $A = \{x_1, x_2,\dots, x_n\}$ any finite subset of $(X, \tau)$. Then $A$ is compact.
:::

**Proof.** Let $O_i$, $i \in I$, be any family of open sets such that $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} O_i$. Then for each $x_j \in A$, there exists an $O_{i_j}$, such that $x_j \in O_{i_j}$. Thus $A \subseteq O_{i_1} \cup O_{i_2} \cup \dots \cup O_{i_n}$. So A is compact.

\vspace{3mm}

In other words, since $A$ is a finite set, we can simply choose one open set for each element in $A$. Then, the union of these carefully selected open sets is automatically a superset of $A$.

::: block
### Remark

So we see from this example that every finite set (in a topological space) is compact. Indeed "compactness" can be thought of as a topological generalization of "finiteness".
:::

## Compactness - Example

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A subset $A$ of a discrete space $(X,\tau)$ is compact $\Longleftrightarrow$ it is finite.
:::

**Proof.** If A is finite then previous example shows that it is compact. Conversely, let $A$ be compact. Then we have the family of singleton sets $O_x = \{x\}$, $x \in A$, such that each $O_x$ is open and $A \subseteq \bigcup_{x\in A}O_x$. As $A$ is compact, there exist $O_{x_1}, O_{x_2},\dots, O_{x_n}$ such that $A\subseteq O_{x_1}\cup O_{x_2}\cup\dots\cup O_{x_n}$ that is, $A \subseteq \{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$. Hence A is a finite set.

\vspace{2mm}

In other words, in a discrete space, every single point has its own open set. If we form an infinite family of open sets where each set contains exactly one point from $A$, their union is clearly a superset of $A$.

By the definition of compactness, we must be able to extract a finite number from these sets whose union is still a superset of $A$. However, since each set holds exactly one point, a finite union can only hold a finite number of points. Thus, $A$ itself must be a finite set.

## Compactness - Open cover

::: block
### Definition 8.2

Let $I$ be a set and $O_i$, $i \in I$, a family of subset of $X$. Let $A$ be a subset of $X$. \vspace{3mm}

\(i\) Then $O_i$, $i \in I$, is said to be a covering (or a cover) of $A$ if $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} O_i$. \vspace{2mm}

\(ii\) If each $O_i$, $i \in I$, is an open set in $(X, \tau)$, then $O_i$, $i \in I$ is said to be an open covering of $A$ if $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} O_i$. \vspace{2mm}

\(iii\) A finite subfamily, $O_{i_1}, O_{i_2},\dots, O_{i_n}$, of $O_i$, $i \in I$, is called a finite subcovering (of $A$) if $A\subseteq O_{i_1}\cup O_{i_2}\cup\dots\cup O_{i_n}$.
:::

## Compactness - Open cover

So we can rephrase the definition of compactness as follows:

::: block
### Definition 8.1

Let $A$ be a subset of a topological space $(X, \tau)$. Then $A$ is said to be compact if for every set $I$ and every family of open sets, $O_i$, $i \in I$, such that $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I}\,O_i$, there exists a finite subfamily $O_{i_1},O_{i_2},\dots,O_{i_n}$ such that $A\subseteq O_{i_1}\cup O_{i_2}\cup \dots \cup O_{i_n}$.
:::

and using definition of open cover:

::: block
### Definition 8.3

A subset $A$ of a topological space $(X, \tau)$ is said to be compact if every open covering of $A$ has a finite subcovering. If the compact subset $A$ equals $X$, then $(X, \tau)$ is said to be a compact space.
:::

## Compact Subset of $\mathbb{R}$

\vspace{3mm}

::: block
### Proposition 8.4

A compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is bounded
:::

**Proof.** Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be unbounded. Then $A \subseteq \bigcup^\infty_{n=1}(-n,n)$, but $\{(-n,n)$ : $n=1,2,3,\dots\}$ does not have any finite subcovering of $A$ as $A$ is unbounded. Therefore $A$ is not compact. Hence all compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are bounded.

::: block
### Proposition 8.5

The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact.
:::

If only finite sets were compact, the study of "compactness" would not be very interesting.

This proposition reveals a powerful fact, even though all finite sets are compact, **not all compact sets are finite**. The interval $[0,1]$ contains an infinite number of points, yet it is compact.

## The Heine-Borel Theorem

\vspace{2mm}

Before diving into the Heine-Borel Theorem itself, we need to establish a few foundational propositions to make the final proof much easier.

First, it is clear that compactness is a **topological property**, since its definition relies entirely on open sets.

However, like we saw last week in connectedness, we don't even need the full strength of a homeomorphism to preserve it.

::: block
### Proposition 8.6

Let $f:X \rightarrow Y$ be a continuous function. If $A$ is a compact subset of $X$, then its image $f(A)$ is compact in $Y$.
:::

**In other words:** A continuous image of a compact set is always compact.

This single proposition leads to several direct consequences.

## The Heine-Borel Theorem

::: block
### Corollary 8.7

Let $f:(X,\tau_X) \rightarrow (Y,\tau_Y)$ be a continuous surjective function. If $(X,\tau_X)$ is compact, then $(Y,\tau_Y)$ is compact.
:::

This corollary scales the previous idea up: a continuous image of an **entire** compact space is also compact.

::: block
### Corollary 8.8

Let $(X,\tau_X)$ and $(Y,\tau_Y)$ be homeomorphic topological spaces. If $(X,\tau_X)$ is compact, then $(Y,\tau_Y)$ is compact.
:::

This confirms that homeomorphism completely preserves compactness across topological spaces.

## The Heine-Borel Theorem

::: block
### Corollary 8.9

For $a$ and $b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, the closed interval $[a,b]$ is compact while the open interval $(a,b)$ is not compact.
:::

The space $[a,b]$ is homeomorphic to $[0,1]$. Since we already proved $[0,1]$ is compact, $[a,b]$ must also be compact (via Corollary 8.8).

The space $(a,b)$ is homeomorphic to $(0,\infty)$. If $(a,b)$ were compact, $(0,\infty)$ would also be compact. But from our very first example, we know $(0,\infty)$ is **not** compact. Hence, $(a,b)$ is not compact.

::: block
### Proposition 8.10

Every closed subset of a compact space is compact.
:::

So only closed subsets of a compact space are guaranteed to be compact, open subsets are not.

## The Heine-Borel Theorem

::: block
### Theorem 8.11 (Heine-Borel Theorem)

Every closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact.
:::

If $A$ is bounded, then $A \subseteq [a, b]$ for some real numbers $a$ and $b$. We already know that $[a, b]$ is compact (from Corollary 8.9).

Since $A$ is a closed subset existing inside a compact space $[a,b]$, $A$ itself must be compact (from Proposition 8.10).

::: block
### Proposition 8.12 (converse of Heine-Borel Theorem)

Every compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed and bounded
:::

This is a direct consequence of Proposition 8.4 (which guarantees it is bounded) and the fundamental properties of the real number line (which guarantee it is closed).

## The Heine-Borel Theorem

\vspace{2mm}

Combining Theorem 8.11 and Proposition 8.12, we can conclude that:

::: block
### Corollary 8.13

A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
:::

Finally, we can generalize this theorem to higher dimensions.

::: block
### Theorem 8.14 (Generalized Heine-Borel Theorem)

A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n≥1$, is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
:::
